finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST /hooks/test forwards attacker-supplied req.body.callback to axios.post with no validation, enabling server-side requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts, with the upstream status code returned to the attacker.
finding.source: req.body.callback (routes.js:20), from an unauthenticated POST to /hooks/test on the pub router (routes.js:19)

trace.note: pub.post("/hooks/test") registered on the public router with no auth middleware
req.body.callback used directly as the axios.post URL; body fixed to {ping:true}, method fixed to POST
res.json({status: r.status}) returns the upstream status to the caller, so the endpoint works as a status-code oracle for internal hosts

finding.guards_checked: No auth middleware on pub (routes.js:19). No URL parsing, scheme allowlist, hostname allowlist, or resolved-IP / private-range check (routes.js:20). No redirect restriction (axios follows redirects by default in Node). No timeout or maxRedirects override. Caveat: whether the app mounts the pub router behind an outer auth layer is not visible in this repo; the router name and the absence of middleware here suggest it is public.

verdict.guard_found: none: routes.js:19-22 has no auth middleware, URL validation, host allowlist, or IP check. The only middleware in the file is admin.use(requireAdmin) at routes.js:12, which applies to the admin router, not pub.
verdict.reason: The code at routes.js:19-20 passes req.body.callback straight to axios.post with no guard, so the SSRF exists if pub is mounted on a public path, but the mount point is not in this repo (routes.js:4 defines the router and nothing here calls app.use with it), so reachability by an unauthenticated attacker cannot be confirmed. The status-oracle part is overstated: axios rejects non-2xx responses by default, so routes.js:21 only returns status for successful or redirected responses.

finding.claim: Admin GET /diagnostics/fetch forwards req.query.url to axios.get with no validation, letting an authenticated admin (or a cross-site request that carries an admin session) make the server fetch arbitrary URLs. Only the status code is returned, so this is blind.
finding.source: req.query.url (routes.js:15), from GET /diagnostics/fetch on the admin router, behind requireAdmin (routes.js:7-12)

trace.note: admin.use(requireAdmin) applies to every route on the admin router
requireAdmin checks req.session.role === "admin" only; it does not constrain the URL
req.query.url passed directly to axios.get; no type check, so non-string values reach the client unchecked
res.json({status: r.status}) returns only the upstream status code

finding.guards_checked: requireAdmin role check (routes.js:7-9, gates access but not the target). No URL parsing, scheme or host allowlist, or IP/DNS check (routes.js:15). No redirect restriction. Severity is lower because the caller must hold an admin session; a cross-site trigger depends on the session cookie's SameSite setting, which is not visible in this repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. requireAdmin (routes.js:7-10) checks only req.session.role === "admin" and does not constrain the URL. Nothing between req.query.url (routes.js:15) and axios.get (routes.js:15) validates scheme, host, or IP, and there is no redirect restriction.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches routes.js:12, 8, 14, 15 and 16, and no closing guard exists, but the source is only attacker-controlled through an admin session (routes.js:8), which is not low-privilege. The cross-site path depends on session cookie SameSite and CSRF protection (routes.js:14 has none visible), and neither is in the repo, so the finding can be neither confirmed nor refuted from this code.
